newsitem.title: UK: "Big L" is back as UK pirate station rocks ashore.
newsitem.headline: "Big L" is back as UK pirate station rocks ashore.

text.p: It's a blast from the past.
Radio London came back on the air on Friday, 30 years after the pirate rock music station was forced to stop its broadcasts from a ship in the North Sea.
"Wonderful Radio London", otherwise known as the "Big L", became a legend of the Swinging Sixties with its diet of non-stop pop and rock music beamed from a converted World War Two minesweeper.
London went on air in 1964 and soon boasted 12 million listeners in Britain and four million in Europe.
But it was one of several unregulated pirate stations that were eventually forced to close in a government clampdown in 1967.
To mark the 30th anniversary of the closure, promoter and sixties pop fan Ray Anderson has resumed broadcasts for 28 days, although this time the station has a licence from Britain's Radio Authority.
The idea is to mark the anniversary, make a bit of money from promotions such as tourist boat trips and to help a few charities.
Original DJs such as Mark Roman, Pete Brady, Keith Skues, Tony Brandon and Ed "Stewpot" Stewart will either be re-creating their original shows from the 1960s or dropping in for guest spots.

Sounds of the sixties will make up the playlist. The original Radio London claimed to be the first radio station in the world to play The Beatles "Sgt Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" as well as "A Whiter Shade of Pale" by Procol Harum.
"This is a great opportunity to bring back the sound of Big L," said Anderson.
"Radio London probably became the most successful commercial station in the world, attracting a huge audience which many of today's commercial broadcasters would envy."
Closing down the pirates opened the door to the British Broadcasting Corporation's Radio One pop station and to officially sanctioned commercial stations in Britain.
Radio London was mourned by fans and DJs were mobbed when they came ashore for the last time after an emotional broadcast on August 14, 1967.

London's original ship, the Galaxy, has been broken up, so the recreated station will be broadcasting, on the original 266 metres medium wave frequency, from a converted cargo vessel, the Yeoman Rose, moored off the east coast resort of Frinton. The station can be heard for a radius of 50 miles (80 kms).
Now, as in the heady days of the 1960s, the playlist features legendary acts such as Tom Jones, Ike and Tina Turner, The Small Faces, The Beach Boys, The Tremeloes, The Kinks and The Who.
